read.text: 7.1 ASSESS FOR ACUTE MALNUTRITION
After assessing the child for general danger signs and the four main symptoms (cough or difficulty breathing, diarrhea, fever and ear problem) then assess all children for Acute Malnutrition

• Assess all children for Signs of acute malnutrition
    • Edema of both feet
    • WFH/L - weight for height (more than 2 years of age) or weight for length (up to 2 years of age)
    • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) in children aged 6 months or more
  • In the presence of signs of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) check for any medical complications and assess appetite or breastfeeding when indicated.
LOOK and FEEL for edema of both feet:

A child with edema of both feet may have kwashiorkor, another form of severeacute malnutrition. Edema is when an unusually large amount of fluid gathers in the child's tissues. The tissues become filled with the fluid and look swollen or puffed up.

Look and feel to determine whether the child has edema of both fetes?. Use your thumb to press gently for a few seconds on the top side of each foot. The child has edema if a dent remains in the child's foot when you lift your thumb.

• classification of edema:
    • +on dorsum of food
    • ++up thigh
    • +++ generalized
ASSESS weight for height or length (WFH/L):

Assess the child's body weight in proportion to attained growth in heightor length.Look now at the example: WHO weight-for-length graph below. The line labeled zero is the median, which is generally speaking, the average. Most healthy children are near the median curve, a little either above or below it. The other lines, called z -score or standard deviations (SD) lines, indicate distance from the average. You will identify children whose weight for length or height is below -3 z-scores curve of the graph; it is the bottom curve of the graph. These children suffer from severe acute malnutrition. You will also identify children whose weight-for-height or length is between -2 and -3 z-scores. These children have moderate acute malnutrition.

• To determine weight-for-height or length:
    • Calculate the child's age in months.
    • Weigh the child (unless the child has already been weighed today). The child should wear light clothing when being weighed.
    • Measure length or height:
      • If a child is less than 2 years old, measure lying down (recumbent) length.
      • If the child is aged 2 years or older and able to stand, measure standing height.
  • NOTE: In general, standing height is about 0.7 cm less than lying down length. Therefore, if a child less than 2 years old will not lie down for measurement of length, measure standing height and add 0.7 cm to convert it to length; if a child aged 2 years or older cannot stand, measure lying down length and subtract 0.7 cm to convert it to Height.

sections.title: MUAC, medical complications and the appetite test

read.text: Measure MUAC, check a child with severe acute malnutrition for medical complications, and do an appetite test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: MEASURE mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)
A quick way of identifying acute malnutrition in children aged 6 months and more is measuring the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC).
To measure the mid upper arm circumference:

items: Use a special tape for measuring MUAC or, if not available, a string
Place the tape or string placed around the upper arm, midway between the tip of shoulder and the tip of bent elbow
Do not to pull the tape or string too tightly To obtain the mid upper arm circumference:
Read the measurement if you used a tape
Measure the string with a ruler if you used a string MUAC interpretation
If MUAC is less than 115 mm - severe acute malnutrition and threat of death
If MUAC is 115 up to 125 mm - moderate acute malnutrition
If MUAC is 125 mm or more – no malnutrition

read.text: CHECK for medical complications

Severely malnourished children who have also medical complications have a high risk of death and need to be treated in a hospital and usually less than 20%of cases of SAM. Check a child that has edema of both feet or MUAC less than 115 mm or WHF/L less than -3 z-scores for medical complications necessitating referral. Medical complications necessitating referral are:

items: Any general danger sign
Any severe classification
Pneumonia with chest indrawing Note: These complications include main symptoms, which would have been already assessed ASSESS appetite

read.caption: Measuring the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC).

items: An important criterion to decide if a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition can be treated at home or needs to be referred to a hospital is the appetite test.
Malnutrition changes the way infections and other diseases express themselves.

Children severely affected by infections or and other diseases, who are malnourished, frequently show no signs of these diseases. Major complications lead to a loss of appetite. A poor appetite means that the child has a significant infection or a major metabolic abnormality such as liver dysfunction, electrolyte imbalance, cell membrane damage, or damaged biochemical pathways. Such child is at immediate risk of death.

read.text: Conducting an appetite test means offering the child Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and assessing whether the child ate at least the amount described below. The appetite test is conducted at the initial visit and each follow-up visit to the health facility. The test usually takes a short time but may take up to 30 minutes.
Conduct an appetite test for a child aged 6 months or more who:

• Has MUAC less than 115 mm OR
  • Has WFH/L less than -3 z- score OR
  • Has edema of both feet AND
  • Does NOT have medical complications. To conduct an appetite test
  • Arrange a quiet corner where the child and mother can take their time to get accustomed to eating the RUTF.
  • The child may not eat the RUTF because he or she is frightened, distressed or fearful of the environment or staff. This is particularly likely if there is a crowd, a lot of noise, other distressed children or intimidating health professionals (white coats, awe-inspiring tone). The appetite test should therefore be conducted a separate quiet area. If a quiet area is not possible then the appetite can be tested outside the clinic.
  • Determine RUFT portion needed to perform the test (1/3 RUTF scatch 92 gram)
  • Explain to the mother:
    • Your child is malnourished and needs to eat the Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) until he or she will grow well again. RUTF is a food and medicine for malnourished children and show her photos of transformation before and after illness.
    • I need to see if your child has a good appetite and will eat the RUTF in sufficient amounts at home. Therefore, I will give you some RUTF and you will feed it to your child now.
  • Advise the mother to:
    • Wash hands before giving the RUTF
    • Sit with the child on her lap and gently offer the child RUTF to eat.
    • Encourage the child to eat the RUTF. If the child refuses, continue to quietly encourage the child and take your time. Do not force the child to eat the RUTF
    • Offer plenty of clean water to drink from a cup when the child is taking the RUTF.
  • After 30 minutes asses the results of appetite test:
  • A child that eat 1/3 amount of RUFT scatch , Pass the appetite test.
  • Now explain to the mother that the child can be treated at home. You will learn how to explain to her how to feed the child at home and when to return for the follow-up visit later in this training.
  • A child that does NOT eat 1/3 amount of RUFT scatch, fails the appetite test.
  • Explain now to the mother that her child needs to eat the RUTF to treat his orher malnutrition but because of poor appetite the child would not take sufficient amounts of the RUTF at home, would continue to get worse, and could even die. For this reason, the child needs to be urgently treated in a hospital. Even if you or the mother think that the child did not take the RUTF because he or she does not like the taste or is frightened, the child still needs to be referred to in-patient care for least a short time. If it is later found that the child actually takes sufficient RUTF to pass the test then he or she can be immediately transferred to the outpatient treatment.

read.text: 8.0 ASSESS AND CLASSIFY ANEMIA

Pallor is unusual paleness of the skin. It is a sign of anemia. Although this clinical sign is less reliable than many other clinical signs, it allows health-care providers to identify sick children with severe anemia, often caused by malaria infection. Where feasible, the specificity of anemia diagnosis may be greatly increased by using a simple laboratory test (e.g. Hb test).
8.1 ASSESS FOR ANEMIA
LOOK for palmar pallor:

items: To see if the child has palmar pallor, look at the skin of the child's palm. Hold the child's palm open by grasping it gently from the side. Do not stretch the fingers backwards, because this may cause pallor by blocking the blood supply.

Compare the color of the child's palm with your own palm and with the palms of other children. If the skin of the child's palm is pale, the child has some palmar pallor. If the skin of the palm is so pale that it looks white, the child has severe palmar pallor.

SEVERE ANAEMIA
If the child has severe palmar pallor, classify the child as having SEVERE ANAEMIA.
ANAEMIA
If the child has some palmar pallor, classify the child as having ANAEMIA.
NO ANAEMIA
If the child does not have palmar pallor, classify the child as having NO ANAEMIA

sections.title: Contraindications to immunization

read.text: Know the only three contraindications, and immunize sick children who are well enough to go home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: OBSERVE CONTRAINDICATIONS TO IMMUNIZATION

In the past, some health workers thought minor illness was a contraindication to immunization (a reason to not immunize the child). They sent sick children away and told the mothers to bring them back when the children are well. This is a bad practice because it delays immunization. The mother may have traveled a long distance to bring her sick child to the clinic and cannot easily bring the child back for immunization at another time. The child is left at risk of getting measles, hepatitis B, Meningitis, polio, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus or tuberculosis.
It is very important to immunize sick and malnourished children against these diseases.
There are only three situations at present, which are contraindications to immunization:

items: 1- Do not give BCG to a child known to have AIDS.
2- Do not give Penta 2 or Penta 3 to a child who has had convulsions or shock within 3 days of the most recent dose.
3- Do not give Penta to a child with recurrent convulsions or another active neurological disease of the central nervous system.

read.text: Note: If DT and HB vaccine are available, given to children in the situation 2 and 3, because most complications of Penta vaccine are associated with pertussis vaccine.

• In all other situations, here is a good rule to follow:
    • There are no contraindications to immunization of a sick child if the Child is well enough to go home.
    • If a child is going to be referred, do not immunize the child before referral. The hospital staff at the referral site should make the decision about immunizing the child when the child is admitted. This will avoid delaying referral.
    • Children with diarrhea who are due for OPV should receive a dose of OPV (oral polio vaccine) during this visit. However, do not count the dose. The child should return in 4 weeks for an extra dose of OPV.
    • Advise the mother to be sure the other children in the family are immunized. Give the mother tetanus toxoid, if required.
    • To decide if the child needs an immunization:
LOOK at the child's age on the clinical record. If you do not already know the child's age, ask about the child's age. ASK the mother if the young infant has an immunization card.

items: If the mother answers YES:
Ask her if she has brought the card to the clinic today.
If she has brought the card with her, ask to see the card.
Compare the young infant immunization record with the recommended immunization schedule. Decide whether the young infant has had all the immunizations recommended for the child's age.
On the Recording Form, check all immunizations the young infant has already received.
Write the date of the immunization the child received most recently. Circle any immunization the child needs.
If the child is not being referred, explain to the mother that the child needs to receive an immunization (or immunizations).
If the mother says that she does NOT have an immunization card with her:
Ask the mother to tell you what immunizations the child has received.
Use your judgment to decide if the mother has given a reliable report. If you have any doubt, immunize the child.

read.text: 8.2 CHECK THE CHILD’S VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION STATUS
Vitamin A is given both to treat and to prevent disease.

items: It is given as treatment to children with measles, or severe malnutrition.
It is given as supplementation to prevent vitamin A deficiency

read.text: Many children in Sudan have some degree of vitamin A deficiency, which does not show. Therefore, giving vitamin A to all children age 6 months or older will prevent vitamin A deficiency. This will of course include children with persistent diarrhea, malnutrition, pneumonia and other illness. In several studies, this approach has been shown to reduce mortality in areas with vitamin A deficiency. Another important way to prevent deficiency is to make sure that infants are breastfed and, that after 6 months of age; they are fed complementary foods, which are rich in vitamin A.
When giving vitamin A as a supplement to prevent deficiency, make sure that it is not given more often than every 6 months.
Record the date on which the vitamin A dose was given on the child’s card.

When supplies of vitamin A are adequate, all children age 6 months up to 5 years should receive vitamin A every 6 months. Visits to clinic for illness are an opportunity to check when the child most recently received vitamin A. If the child is age 6 months or older and has not received vitamin A in the previous 6 months, give a single dose of vitamin A in the clinic.
Giving vitamin A for treatment of measles or severe malnutrition is the most important use. If vitamin A supplies are limited, use what vitamin A you have to treat children with these illnesses.
VITAMIN A SUPPLEMENTATION STATUS:
Is child age 6 months or older? Has child received a dose of vitamin A in the previous 6 months?
To check the child’s vitamin A supplementation status:

• Look at the child’s age. You will only give vitamin A supplementation if the child is 6 months or older.
  • Look at the child’s card:
    • See if there is a record of previous vitamin A doses.
    • If no vitamin A has been given in the last 6 months, the child should receive a dose.
    • Circle the Vitamin A Supplementation box on the Recording Form.
Check yourself
A child 10 months old received vitamin A 2 months ago. Does he need vitamin A supplementation today?
read.explanation: When giving vitamin A as a supplement to prevent deficiency, make sure that it is not given more often than every 6 months.

read.text: A child 4 months old has never had vitamin A. Does he need vitamin A supplementation today?
read.explanation: You will only give vitamin A supplementation if the child is 6 months or older.

• 1. Introduction In the previous module you learned to assess the sick child age 2 months up to 5years and to classify the child's illness or illnesses. The next step is to identify the necessary treatments. In some instances, the very sick child will need referral to a hospital for additional care. If so, you will begin urgent treatments before the child's departure.
  • 2. Learning objectives This module will describe and allow you to practice the following skills:

  • identifying treatments needed
  • For patients who need urgent referral:
    • identifying the urgent pre-referral treatments
    • explaining the need for referral to the mother

For example, find PNEUMONIA and read its treatments; then diarrhoea with NO DEHYDRATION; then DYSENTERY. Severe classifications usually require referral: “Refer URGENTLY to hospital”. This module does not describe how to do the treatments, only how to identify which treatments are needed.

read.text: In this module you will use the "identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart. If a child has only one classification, it is easy to see what to do for the child. However, many children have more than one classification

When a child has more than one classification, you must look at more than one place on the ASSESS and CLASSIFY chart to see the treatments listed. The coloured rows help you to quickly identify treatment.
A classification in a pink row means that the child needs urgent referral or admission for inpatient care. This is a severe classification

A classification in a yellow row means that the child needs an appropriate oral drug or other treatment. The treatment includes teaching the mother how to give oral drugs or to treat local infections at home. You also must advise her about caring for the child at home and when she should return

A classification in a green row means that the child does not need specific medical treatment such as antibiotics. Teach the child's caretaker how to care for the child at home. For example, you might advise her on feeding her sick child or giving fluid for diarrhoea. Then teach her signs indicating when the child should return immediately to the health facility

For some classifications, the treatment column says: "Refer urgently to hospital." Hospital means a health facility with inpatient beds, supplies and expertise to treat a very sick child. If your health facility has inpatient beds, referral may mean admission to the inpatient department of that facility. If an infant or child must be referred urgently, you must decide which treatments to do before referral. Some treatments (such as wicking an ear) are not necessary before referral. This section will help you to identify urgent pre-referral treatments

If there is no hospital in the area, you may make some decisions differently than as described in this unit. If referral is not possible, or if the parents refuse to take the child to the hospital, you should help the family care for the child. The child may stay near the clinic to be seen several times a day. Or a health worker may visit the home to help give drugs on schedule and to help give fluids and food

read.text: 3.2 Referral for general danger signs
Most children who have a general danger sign also have a severe classification. They will be referred for their severe classification (or possibly treated if they have SEVERE DEHYDRATION only).

In rare instances, children may have general danger signs without a severe classification. These children should be referred urgently. There is a box at the bottom of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart to remind you:
MAKE SURE A CHILD WITH ANY GENERAL DANGER SIGN IS

REFERRED after first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and other urgent pre-referral treatments. Exception: Rehydration of the child according to Plan C may resolve danger signs so that referral is no longer needed.
REFERRAL FOR OTHER SEVERE PROBLEMS
The ASSESS and CLASSIFY chart does not include all problems that children may have. You must ask yourself:
Does the child have any other severe problem that cannot be treated in this clinic?
For example, the child may have a severe problem that is not covered on the chart, such as severe abdominal pain. If you cannot treat a severe problem, you will need to refer the child.

Remember: Most children will have none of the general danger signs, severe classification, or other severe problems. If the child has none of these, the child dose not need urgent referral to a hospital. You will identify treatments needed as described in section 4.0 of this module.

items: 4. Identify treatments for patients who do not need urgent referral

read.text: Your facilitator will present the example in this section and will show you how to use the back of the Sick Child Recording Form. The facilitator will show you how to: Fold the "classify" column of the Sick Child Recording Form so that you can see it while looking at the back of the form.
4.1 Identify treatment
Look at the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart to find the treatments needed for each of the child's classifications. List each treatment needed on the back of the Sick Child Recording Form

For each classification listed on the front of the Sick Child’s Recording Form, you will write the treatments needed on the back of the form. The treatments that may be needed are in the "Identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart. You will list only the treatments that apply to the specific child being treated.

Be sure to include items that begin with the words "Follow-up." These mean to tell the mother to return in a certain number of days. The follow-up visit is very important to see if the treatment is working or not, and give another treatment if needed. You may abbreviate follow-up as "F/up."

If several different times are specified for follow-up, you will look for the earliest definite time. (A definite time is one that is not followed by the word "if"). For example: "Follow-up in 3 days" gives a definite time for follow-up. "Follow-up in 3 days if fever persists" is not definite. The child only needs to come back if fever persists.

Record the earliest definite time for follow-up in the appropriate space on the back of the Sick Child Recording Form. This is the follow-up visit to tell the mother about. (Also tell her about any earlier follow-up that may be needed if a condition such as fever persists.) Later, when the mother returns for follow-up, you can tell her about any additional visits needed.

Also be sure to list non-urgent referrals for further assessment. For example, for cough which has lasted more than 14 days, or for fever, which has lasted 7 days or more, you would record, "Refer for assessment." Although the mother should take the child for assessment promptly, these causes of referral are not so urgent. Any other necessary treatments may be done before referral. You must teach the mother when to return immediately according to the appropriate classification and list them on the recording form. You will need to teach each mother the signs that mean she should return immediately for more care for her child. You will learn these signs later in this module. Note: you will learn to complete the feeding sections of the Sick Child Recording Form in the module COUNSEL THE MOTHER. When feeding assessment is needed, it may be done at any convenient time during the visit, after the child's immediate needs are taken care of. Some treatments are listed for more than one problem. If a patient has two problems that needed the same drug, you need only to the write the drug once on your Sick Child Recording Form. However, if an antibiotic is needed for more than one problem, you should list it each time. When the same antibiotic is appropriate for two different problems, you can give that single antibiotic, but two problems may require different antibiotics. You will learn about choosing antibiotics in the Treat the Child.
Most instructions in the "Identify Treatment" column of the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart are easily understood. However, there are some instructions that require special explanation:

items: ANAEMIA A child with palmer pallor should begin iron treatment for ANAEMIA (make sure that the child has no sickle cell anemia and not receive RUTF). Give mebendazole if child is 1 year or older.

read.text: 4.2 When to return immediately:

sections.title: Identify urgent pre-referral treatments

read.text: Identify the urgent treatments to give before referral, and the ones that must not delay it.
read.label: In this lesson

items: 5. Identify treatment if urgent referral is needed

read.text: 5.1 identify urgent pre-referral treatment needed

When a child needs urgent referral, you must quickly identify and begin the most urgent treatments for that child. The following are urgent treatments. They are in bold print on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart, you will give just the first dose of the drugs before referral:

items: Give diazepam to a child who is convulsing now.
Give quinine for VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE.
Give an appropriate antibiotic.
Give vitamin A for treatment of measles.
Treat the child to prevent low blood sugar (This involves giving breast milk, milk, or sugary water as described on the TREAT chart.)
Give rapid bronchodilator to treat wheeze.
Give paracetamol for high fever (38.5°C or above) or pain from mastoiditis.
Apply tetracycline eye ointment (if clouding of the cornea or pus draining from eye)
Provide ORS solution so that the mother can give frequent sips on the way to the hospital.

read.text: The first six treatments above are urgent because they can prevent serious consequences such as progression of bacterial meningitis or cerebral malaria, corneal rupture due to lack of vitamin A, or brain damage from low blood sugar or low oxygen level. The other listed treatments are also important to prevent worsening of the illness.

Do not delay referral to give non-urgent treatments such as wicking the ear or oral iron treatment. If immunizations or vitamin A supplementation are needed, do not give it before referral. Let hospital personnel to determine when to give immunizations and vitamin A supplement for prevention. This will avoid delaying referral. Give vitamin A when it is needed for treatment of a child with MEASLES.
EXAMPLE:

Nagla is a 15-month-old girl. She has COUGH OR COLD. She has fever of 38.2°C and stiff neck, so she is classified as having VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE, NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION AND NO ANEMIA and has no other classifications.
Nagla needs urgent referral. Before going to the hospital, she should be given:

items: Quinine (first dose).
Appropriate antibiotic (first dose).
Treatment to prevent low blood sugar.

read.text: The health worker should NOT take time to teach how to soothe the throat and relieve the cough with a safe remedy since that is not an urgent treatment. The health worker should NOT take time to assess feeding and counsel the mother on feeding.

read.text: 5.2 Give urgent pre-referral treatment

The next module will describe how to do treatments presented on the TREAT chart. All urgent, Pre-referral treatments are included on that chart. When referring a child, do the treatments quickly. Do not take time to teach the mother as you would in a non-urgent situation.

Many severe cases need the first dose of an antibiotic before referral. However, if a child cannot drink, is vomiting everything, is having convulsions, or cannot be wakened, the child will not be able to take an oral antibiotic, other oral drugs, or drinks such as ORS or breast milk. The child with these danger signs will need to be given an intramuscular injection antibiotic instead of an oral antibiotic. Dosages will be known in the next module. ORS or oral drugs such as paracetamol will need to be given in the hospital when the child is able to take them. If the child needs treatment to prevent low blood sugar, and you are able to insert an NG tube, give sugar water or breast milk substitute by NG tube before referral.
5.3 Refer the child
Do four steps to refer a child to the hospital:

• 1. Explain to the mother the need for referral, and get her agreement to take the child. If you suspect that she does not want to take the child, find out why? Possible reasons are:
    • She thinks that hospitals are places where people often die, and she fears that her child will die there too.
    • She does not think that the hospital will help the child.
    • She cannot leave home to take care of her sick child during a hospital stay because:
      • there is no one to take care of her other children, or
      • she is needed for farming, or
      • she may lose a job.
    • She does not have money to pay for transportation, hospital bills, medicines, or food during the hospital stay.
  • 2. Calm the mother’s fears and help her to resolve any problem. For example:
    • If the mother fears that her child will die in the hospital, reassure her that the hospital has Specialists, and equipment that can help cure her child
    • Explain what will happen in the hospital and how that will help her child.
    • If the mother needs help at home while she is in the hospital, ask questions and make suggestions about who could help. For example, ask whether her husband, sister or mother could help with the other children or with meals while she is away.
    • Discuss with mother how she can travel to the hospital. Help arranging transportation if necessary.

You may not be able to help the mother solving her problems and be sure that she will go to the hospital. However, it is important to do everything you can to help. If referral is not possible, there are some things you can do for the child from your clinic. These are described in an annex of the module Treat the Child.

items: 3. Write a referral note for the mother to take with her to the hospital to give the health worker there.

read.text: Write in referral note:

• The date and time of referral
  • Name and age of the child
  • Name of Hospital that you will refer to.
  • Description of the child’s problem,
  • Reason for referral (symptoms and signs leading to severe classification)
  • Treatment that you have given
  • Any other information that the health worker in the hospital needs to know in order to care for the child, such as previous treatment of the illness or immunizations needed
  • Your name and the name of your clinic.
  • 4. Give the mother any supplies and instructions needed to care for her child on the way to the hospital:
    • If the hospital is too far, give the mother additional doses of antibiotic and tell her when to give them during the trip (according to dosage schedule on TREAT chart).
    • If you think that the mother will not actually go to the hospital, give her the full course of antibiotics, and teach her how to give them.
    • Tell the mother how to keep the young child warm during the trip.
    • Advise the mother to continue breastfeeding.
    • If the child has some or severe dehydration and can drink, give the mother some ORS solution for the child to sip frequently on the way.

Because Nadia's mother said the child felt hot, and because her temperature is 38.5 C, the health worker assessed her for fever. Nadia lives where there is high malaria risk. She has had fever for 5 days. Her rash is generalized rash, and she has red eyes. She has measles. She does not have a stiff neck. The health worker assessed her for signs of measles complications. Nadia does not have mouth ulcers. There is no pus draining from the eye and no clouding of the cornea. Nadia does not have an ear problem. The health worker next checked her for malnutrition or anemia. She does not have edema of both feet. The health worker determined her weight for length. Then checked for anemia and found no palmar pallor.

She has a generalized rash and no complications: MEASLES.
MUAC 11 cm (less than 115 mm), no oedema, no medical complication, and she passed the appetite test: UNCOMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION.
No palmar pallor: NO ANAEMIA.

questions.question: If the child is being referred for severe classification
options: Immunize this child today if due for immunization

options: Immunize this child today if due for immunization

narrative: Najwa is 4 months old. She weighs 5.5 kg. Her length is 60 cm, her temperature is 38.0 C.She is in the clinic today because she has diarrhea, she does not have any general danger signs. She is not coughing and does not have difficulty breathing. The health worker assessed her further for signs of diarrhea. She has had diarrhea for 2 days and there is blood in the stool, said the mother. Najwa was not restless or irritable; she was not unconscious or lethargic. Her eyes were not sunken. She drank normally, and did not seem to be thirsty. Her skin pinch went back immediately. The health worker next assessed her for fever. Najwa has had fever for 2 days, said the mother. She has not had measles in the last 3 months. She does not have a stiff neck. She has runny nose. There are no signs suggesting measles and malaria rapid diagnostic test was negative Najwa does not have an ear problem. The health worker checked her for sever acute malnutrition and anemia. She does not have oedema of both feet; the health worker determined her weight for height. Had no palmer pallor. At birth, Najwa received BCG and OPV 0. Four weeks ago, she received Penta 1 and OPV 1 PCV1 ROTA1.
learningPoints: No signs of dehydration: NO DEHYDRATION. Blood in the stool: DYSENTERY.
Fever with a negative malaria test: FEVER NO MALARIA.
Weight for length (5.5 kg, 60 cm, girl): -2 z-scores or more: NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION. She is 4 months old: MUAC is not used.
No palmar pallor: NO ANAEMIA.
Immunization: she needs Penta 2, OPV 2, PCV 2 and Rota 2 today. No vitamin A: she is under 6 months.

exercises.title: Sudan IMNCI: Exercise R, case 3: Jamila
exercises.source: Sudan IMNCI module: Assess and classify the sick child (2023)
narrative: Jamila is 37 months old. She weighs 15.3 kg. height 80 cm, her temperature is 38.5 C. Jamila's family brought her to the clinic today because she has a stomachache, feels hot, has a runny nose andrash and she is coughing. The health worker checked her for general danger signs. She was able to drink, did not vomit everything she drank, did not have convulsions, and was not lethargic or unconscious. The health worker assessed the child for cough or difficult breathing. The parents said she has been coughing for 2 days. The health worker counted 55 breaths a minute. He did not see chest indrawing. He did not hear any unusual noise when she breathed in or out. Jamila does not have diarrhea, said the parents. However, she has been feeling hot, they said. The risk of malaria is high. She has had fever for two days. She has not had measles in the last 3 months. Her neck moves easily. The health worker looked for signs suggesting measles. Her rash was not generalized; it was only on her hand. Malaria test was positive. Jamila did not have an ear problem, said the parents. The health worker checked Jamila for malnutrition and anemia. She does not have edema of both feet. The health worker determined her weight for age. MUAC 13 cm. She does not have palmar pallor. Jamila has received BCG, OPV 0, OPV 1, OPV 2, OPV 3, Penta 1, Penta 2, and Penta 3 PCV1 PCV2 PCV3 and ROTA1 ROTA 2. Jamila has received vitamin A supplementation one month ago.
learningPoints: 37 months old with 55 breaths per minute: fast breathing, PNEUMONIA.
Fever and a positive malaria test: MALARIA. Her rash is only on her hand, not generalized: do not classify measles.
MUAC 13 cm: NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION. No palmar pallor: NO ANAEMIA.
She is up to date for her age except measles, yellow fever and Men A, which the book's history does not list; she had vitamin A one month ago, so no vitamin A today.

exercises.title: Sudan IMNCI: Identify treatment, Exercise A: is urgent referral needed?
exercises.source: Sudan IMNCI module: Identify treatment (2023)
narrative: In this exercise you will decide whether or not urgent referral is needed. Tick the appropriate answer.

questions.question: 1. Neema is a 6-month-old girl. She has no general danger signs. She has: o COUGH OR COLD o DIARRHEA with NO DEHYDRATION o PERSISTENT DIARRHOEA o NO ACUTE SEVER MALNUTRTION o NO ANAEMIA Does Neema need an urgent referral? Yes ____ No____
questions.explain: No. Neema has no general danger signs and no severe classifications.

questions.question: 2. Daoud is a 7- month-old boy. He has no general danger signs. He has: o MASTOIDITIS o MALARIA o NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION o NO ANAEMIA Does Daoud need urgent referral? Yes ____ No ____
questions.explain: Yes. Daoud has a severe classification: MASTOIDITIS.

questions.question: 3. Maher is a 2- years -old boy. He had convulsions this morning and is not eating well. He has: o NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION o NO ANAEMIA Does Maher need urgent referral? Yes ____ No ____
questions.explain: Yes. Maher has a general danger sign: convulsions.

questions.question: 4. Habib is a 9-months -old boy. He is lethargic. He has: o Diarrhoea with SEVERE DEHYDRATION o NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION o NO ANAEMIA. The clinic can provide IV therapy Does Habib need urgent referral? Yes _____ No____
questions.explain: No. Habib's general danger sign may be related to dehydration, and his only severe classification is SEVERE DEHYDRATION. Since this clinic can give IV therapy, Habib should be given IV therapy at the clinic.

questions.question: 5. Ibrahim is a 15-month-old child. Ibrahim is not able to drink. He has: o Diarrhoea with SEVERE DEHYDRATION, o NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION, o NO ANEMIA The clinic cannot provide IV therapy nor NG therapy. Does Ibrahim need urgent referral? Yes _____ No ____
questions.explain: Yes. His only severe classification is SEVERE DEHYDRATION, so use Plan C. The clinic cannot provide IV or NG therapy and he cannot drink: refer him for IV therapy.

exercises.title: Sudan IMNCI: Identify treatment, Exercise B: treatments for Mai
exercises.source: Sudan IMNCI module: Identify treatment (2023)
narrative: In this exercise you will identify treatments for children who do not need urgent referral. Mai is 16-month-old, she has: No general danger signs FEVER- NO MALARIA (fever 38.5 °C; In clinic, ICT for malaria negative, fever present for 4 days), MEASLES WITH EYE COMPLICAIONS (pus draining from eye), NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION NO ANAEMIA. May has received BCG and 3 doses of (Penta ¸PCV and OPV) and 2 Rota doses.

questions.question: A. What treatments are needed for FEVER- NO MALARIA?
points: Give one dose of paracetamol in clinic for high fever (38.5°C or above).
Give appropriate antibiotic treatment for an identified bacterial cause of fever.
Advise the mother when to return immediately.
Follow-up in 3 days if fever persists.

questions.question: B. What treatments are needed for MEASLES WITH EYE COMPLICATIONS?
points: Give vitamin A treatment.
If pus draining from the eye, treat eye infection with tetracycline eye ointment.
Follow-up in 3 days.

questions.question: C. Look in the "Identify Treatment" column for NO ANAEMIA.
points: If child is less than 2 years old, assess the child's feeding and counsel the mother according to the feeding recommendations.
If feeding problem, follow-up in 5 days.

questions.question: D. Does May need a feeding assessment?
questions.explain: Yes, because she is less than 2 years old.

questions.question: E. What immunization does May need?
points: Measles immunization (and, by the schedule, the other 9-month vaccines: yellow fever and Men A).

questions.question: F. Should she be given vitamin (A) supplementation today?
questions.explain: Yes, she should receive vitamin A supplementation.

questions.question: G. What is earliest definite time for May to return for follow-up?
questions.explain: 3 days.

exercises.title: Sudan IMNCI: Identify treatment, Exercise D: urgent pre-referral treatments
exercises.source: Sudan IMNCI module: Identify treatment (2023)
narrative: In this exercise you will practice identifying urgent pre-referral treatments; Remember that these are in bold print on the ASSESS& CLASSIFY chart.

questions.question: 1. Nora is a 15-month-old girl. She has no general danger signs. She has: COUGH OR COLD, MASTOIDITS, NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION and NO ANAEMIA, and no other classifications. Nora needs urgent referral for MASTOIDITIS. Following is a list of treatments for all Nora’s classifications. Tick the urgent, pre-referral treatment(s): (Tick all that apply.)
options: a. soothe the throat and relieve cough with a safe remedy.
b. Advise the mother when to return immediately.
c. Follow-up in 5days if not better.
d. Give first dose of an appropriate antibiotic.
e. Give first dose of paracetamol for pain.
g. Assess the child’s feeding and counsel the mother on feeding. If feeding problem, follow-up in 5 days.
questions.explain: d, e and f. Soothing the throat is not urgent; the hospital will explain when to return and about follow-up; there is no time or need to assess feeding before referral.

questions.question: 2. Hanan is an 18-month-old girl. She has no general danger signs. She has NO SIGNS OF DEHYDRATION OR PERSISTENT DIARRHIEA, COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRTION, NO ANAEMIA, and no other classifications. Hanan needs urgent referral for COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRTION Following is a list of treatments for all Hanan’s classifications. Tick the urgent, pre- referral treatment(s): (Tick all that apply.)
options: a) Give fluid and food to prevent dehydration (plan A).
b) Advise the mother when to return immediately.
c) Advise the mother on feeding a child who has persistent diarrhoea.
g) Treat to prevent low blood sugar.
questions.explain: e and f (the facilitator guide's answer), and g: treatment to prevent low blood sugar is one of the urgent treatments in this module's list. Plan A is not urgent and takes considerable time; the hospital will explain feeding, follow-up and when to return.

questions.question: 3. Omer is a 2-year-old boy. He is lethargic. has a fever of 39°C. The health worker classifies Omer as having VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE and CHRONIC EAR INFECTION. He has some palmar pallor so is classified as having ANAEMIA, although he is also classified as NO ACUTE MALNUTRTION Omer needs urgent referral for VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE. Following is a list of treatments for all Omer’s classifications. Tick the urgent, pre- referral treatment(s): (Tick all that apply.)
options: a) Give quinine for very severe febrile disease (first dose).
b) Give first dose of an appropriate antibiotic.
c) Treat the child to prevent low blood sugar.
d) Give one dose of paracetamol in clinic for high fever (38.5°C or above).
f) Dry the ear by wicking
h) Assess the child’s feeding and counsel the mother on feeding. If feeding problem, follow-up in 5 days.
k) Advise mother when to return immediately.
questions.explain: a to e. Wicking takes a long time and is not urgent. Iron is not urgent. Since quinine is given, an oral antimalarial is not needed. The hospital will explain follow-up and when to return.

questions.question: 4- Study the following Sick Recording From for Abbas On the back of the recording form, write only the urgent pre-referral treatments. These are in bold print on the ASSESS & CLASSIFY chart. Abbas: 15 months, 9 kg, 39°C, cough for 6 days with 38 breaths per minute, a generalized rash of measles with clouding of the cornea, and a positive malaria test. Classified COUGH OR COLD, MALARIA, MEASLES WITH SEVERE COMPLICATIONS, NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION, NO ANAEMIA.
points: Vitamin A.
First dose of an appropriate antibiotic.
Tetracycline eye ointment (clouding of the cornea).
Paracetamol for high fever (39°C).
Oral antimalarial (first dose) for MALARIA, as in the facilitator guide's answer.
Refer URGENTLY to hospital.
Not before referral: soothe the throat, follow-up, when to return, feeding assessment.

exercises.title: Sudan IMNCI: Identify treatment, Exercise E: Sulieman's referral
exercises.source: Sudan IMNCI module: Identify treatment (2023)
narrative: In this exercise you will review the steps related to referral through a case study. You will use the same case study in a role-play. First, study the Sick Child Recording Form for Sulieman on the next page. Sulieman is 4 months old and is exclusively breastfed.

questions.question: 1. Should Sulieman be referred urgently? Why or why not?
points: By the Recording Form printed in this book: PNEUMONIA (54 breaths per minute, no chest indrawing circled), NO DEHYDRATION, MALARIA, NO ACUTE MALNUTRITION, NO ANAEMIA, and no general danger sign: no severe classification, so no urgent referral.
The facilitator guide's answer: Sulieman should be referred for SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (cough, chest indrawing, fast breathing). Your facilitator tells you which to use.

questions.question: 2. What urgent, pre-referral treatments are needed? Record these on the back of the Sick Child Recording Form.
points: If referred: the first dose of an antibiotic (amoxicillin) and an antimalarial (ALu), as in the facilitator guide.
Do not give immunizations before referral: write that he needs OPV 2 and Penta 2 (and PCV 2 and Rota 2).

questions.question: 3. Write a referral note for Sulieman to a hospital. Use today’s date and the current time. Use your own name as that of the health worker.
points: Today's date and the current time; Urgent referral to (the hospital).
Sulieman, age 4 months.
Reason: SEVERE PNEUMONIA OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE: cough, chest indrawing, fast breathing 54 breaths per minute; also MALARIA, temperature 38°C.
Has been given: amoxicillin and ALu.
Needs: Penta 2 and OPV 2.
Your name and your clinic.
